common_name: Siloam Bertie Ferris Daylily (Miniature Deep Rose Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring (or early fall in mild climates) in well-drained soil amended with compost; this Pauline Henry Siloam miniature forms a dense, floriferous clump and benefits from full sun for the richest eyezone contrast.

directions: Registered by Pauline Henry in 1981, this Siloam-series miniature carries deep rose-shrimp petals set off by a darker rose eyezone and a green throat on blooms under three inches across. It became the very first recipient of the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award in 1985, an honor created specifically to recognize outstanding eyed and banded daylilies. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to keep bloom counts high, and deadhead spent scapes to tidy the planting. Its compact habit and heavy scapes make it a strong candidate for edging beds or small-space perennial borders.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) Don C. Stevens Award records

common_name: Will Return Daylily (Peachy Pink Purple-Haloed Evergreen Daylily)

planting.note: Set out divisions in spring in a sunny, well-drained bed; as an evergreen-foliage cultivar it keeps growing later into fall and benefits from mild-winter or warm-summer climates where the crown won't experience hard freeze-thaw heaving.

directions: Hybridized by W. Spalding and registered in 1983, 'Will Return' bears peachy-pink blooms nearly five inches across, each marked with a purple halo around a green throat on an evergreen plant. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Don C. Stevens Award in 1988, given annually for the most outstanding eyed or banded cultivar. Extended daytime bloom means individual flowers stay open longer than many daylilies, so the midseason flower show reads fuller for longer. Keep plants well watered during the active growing season and top-dress with compost in spring to support the heavier evergreen foliage mass through winter dormancy breaks.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) Don C. Stevens Award records

common_name: Suzy Cream Cheese Daylily (Peach Spider Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; the long narrow spider petals need open air circulation around the clump to display their twist without being shaded out by neighboring perennials.

directions: Bred by Dan Bachman and registered in 2001, this spider-form daylily is a peach self with a gold-yellow throat, its narrow, gracefully twisting petals giving the flower its characteristic airy look. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Harris Olson Spider Award in 2012, the annual recognition for the most outstanding spider-form cultivar with a petal length-to-width ratio of at least 4 to 1. Grow in full sun for the strongest scape and heaviest bloom count, and stake tall scapes in windy sites since spider forms often carry an especially long bloom stalk. Deadhead spent flowers daily during peak bloom to keep the display looking fresh.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) Harris Olson Spider Award records

common_name: Wild Wookie Daylily (Red Tetraploid Spider Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; as a tetraploid spider it produces sturdy, heavy scapes that benefit from slightly richer soil than diploid daylilies to support the larger flower mass.

directions: Hybridized by Pat Stamile and registered in 2002, 'Wild Wookie' is a tetraploid spider daylily carrying a red self above a yellow throat, with petals held in the classic 4-to-1 length-to-width spider proportion. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Harris Olson Spider Award in 2013. Divide every three to four years once clumps become congested, since tetraploid daylilies tend to bulk up quickly and can crowd out neighboring plantings. Full sun brings out the richest red saturation; afternoon shade in the hottest climates can help blooms last longer into the day.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) Harris Olson Spider Award records

common_name: Mascara Snake Daylily (Dark Maroon Chartreuse-Throated Spider Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; this is a tall, late-season semi-evergreen spider, so site it toward the back of the border where its height won't shade shorter companions and where mild-winter gardeners can let the foliage persist.

directions: Bred by Dan Bachman and registered in 2002, 'Mascara Snake' is a diploid spider daylily with dark red-maroon petals streaked by chartreuse midribs above a chartreuse throat, held on scapes that can reach nearly five feet tall with blooms around nine inches across at a dramatic 5-to-1 spider ratio. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Harris Olson Spider Award in 2018. Blooming late in the season, it extends the daylily display after earlier cultivars have finished; give it room at the back of a sunny border and stake if needed given the unusually tall scapes.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) Harris Olson Spider Award records

common_name: Opa Klaus Daylily (Ruffled Butternut Yellow Double Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; deadhead and keep evenly watered through its early-midseason bloom to encourage the later rebloom this tetraploid double is known for.

directions: Hybridized by Bill Waldrop and registered in 2015, 'Opa Klaus' is a tetraploid double daylily in a brilliant butternut yellow, with heavily ruffled edges on nearly every petal of its ten-inch blooms. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ida Munson Award in 2022, the annual honor for the most outstanding double-flowered cultivar, after earlier taking an Honorable Mention and Award of Merit. Semi-evergreen foliage and a tendency to rebloom make it a strong extended-season performer; divide every few years once clumps thicken to keep flower counts high.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) Ida Munson Award records

common_name: Honey Crunch Cupcake Daylily (Lavender-Blend Double Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; this nocturnal-blooming rebloomer opens in late afternoon and holds into the next day, so site it where it can be enjoyed in evening light.

directions: Bred by Tim Herrington and registered in 1999, 'Honey Crunch Cupcake' is a double daylily in a light lavender blend with a darker eye above a honey-gold and green throat, blooming around four inches across on 26-inch scapes. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ida Munson Award in 2019 for the most outstanding double-flowered cultivar, after earlier recognition including an Honorable Mention. Its nocturnal, reblooming habit extends color into the evening and later in the season; divide congested clumps every three to four years and keep soil consistently moist during active growth for the best double form.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) Ida Munson Award records

common_name: Siloam David Kirchhoff Daylily (Pink Orchid Small-Flowered Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; as a dormant-foliage Siloam cultivar it benefits from a winter chill period and performs reliably in colder zones as well as the warm-summer South.

directions: Registered by Pauline Henry in 1986 and named for hybridizer David Kirchhoff, this Siloam-series daylily bears pink-orchid blooms around three and a half inches across, each marked with a sharp cerise pencil eyezone above a green throat. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Annie T. Giles Award, given for the most outstanding small-flowered cultivar between three and four and a half inches in diameter. Blooming early to midseason on a compact, dormant-foliage plant, it suits small-space borders and container culture; divide every three to four years as clumps thicken to maintain strong bloom counts.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) Annie T. Giles Award records

common_name: Golden Scroll Daylily (Fragrant Gold Ruffled Dormant Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun; this dormant-foliage cultivar needs a real winter chill to perform its best and rewards gardeners with fragrance carried well beyond the immediate planting on warm evenings.

directions: Hybridized by Guidry and registered in 1983, 'Golden Scroll' carries large, ruffled, circular blooms over four and a half inches across in a rich gold with tangerine-melon tones on a dormant-foliage plant. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's L. Ernest Plouf Award in 1989, the annual honor for the most consistently fragrant dormant daylily. Reblooming through the season and noticeably scented at dusk, it works well near patios and walkways where its fragrance can be appreciated; divide every few years once the clump becomes crowded to keep bloom production strong.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) L. Ernest Plouf Award records

common_name: Big Fuss Daylily (Large Salmon Double Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; the large double blooms are heavy, so consistent moisture during bud development helps the flowers open fully and hold their form.

directions: Bred by Jan Joiner and registered in 2013, 'Big Fuss' produces large double blooms in salmon with a yellow-to-orange throat, living up to its name with an especially full, ruffled petal count. It won the American Hemerocallis Society's Ida Munson Award, the annual recognition for the most outstanding double-flowered cultivar, after earlier taking an Honorable Mention and Award of Merit. Divide every three to four years as clumps mature to sustain strong bloom counts, and deadhead spent scapes to keep the planting looking neat through the growing season.
sources: American Hemerocallis Society (AHS/American Daylily Society) Ida Munson Award records
